stories.title_en: OBS Studio 33

comments.author: schrodingersket
comments.text:
I haven't spent much time in the video processing/streaming space, but I was delighted to discover OBS Studio this week while putting together what has turned out to be an incredibly cozy little entertainment setup by feeding the two gaming consoles and geriatric gaming desktop I've acquired over the years into an HDMI switcher and USB HDMI capture box that in turn streams the feed into an OBS Studio preview (launched from Steam) running on a dummy display.
Launching OBS Studio through Steam lets me stream that preview to my VR headset over a 6GHz WiFi dongle and play games wirelessly in what feels like my own little private theatre. OBS Studio was the puzzle piece I hadn't figured out when the headset showed up last weekend, and I've been really impressed by its performance so far... I think this setup even shaved some latency off when playing online, since consolidating the consoles next to the router let me hardwire them.
Many many thanks to the OBS Studio team for making software that's helping me live out a small part of what I remember hoping technology could be like back in the 90s. I am grateful (:

Thanks, but no thanks?
I use GrapheneOS, but if you as a bank want to gate access to my money via some kind of technology, you better be including it as part of the account.
For example, HSBC continues to let me manage my bank account via the web browser, and continues to offer a battery powered hardware token as the means of authentication.
I let you hold my money, for whatever reason. Why do you expect me to be your distributed infrastructure provider? I am not going to let you require that I run your proprietary malware in order to access my own money.
The idea where you are effectively _expected_ to constantly provide free compute for companies to run their complete garbage on hardware _you own_ just for the privilege of giving them money is one of the most absurd trend in recent times.
I'd say that JS webapps are the same but at least there you run things on your terms in a sandbox that you can inspect and look at the requests, and there's no effective enclave carved out of your hardware (except for EME but that's another topic for another day and I'd be complaining if banks started to use it too).

You define the syntax tree once, then parse, validate, or pretty-print messages against that structure.
It works by converting the syntax tree to a state machine of possible transitions between segments.

stories.title_en: How close can pure functional programming get to C?

comments.author: jandrewrogers
comments.text:
Much of the difference in optimizability is that C/C++ allows you to do fairly extreme copy elision. This is important because memory bandwidth tends to be a major performance bottleneck.
C/C++ code can trivially reach into some remote bit of state and mutate it directly. The compiler rarely objects, no matter how ugly the access method or pattern. It is up to the programmer to make sure the invariants hold and the compiler can’t always see through it. These elided copies add up, though it usually has a maintainability and safety cost.
It is related to why functional languages tend to be mediocre for supercomputing in practice despite having nice properties for massive parallelism in theory.

stories.title_en: How to run a city builder on 16 MHz

comments.author: prosaic-hacker
comments.text:
This is a good revelation but is a technique that is old as the hills.  My first post university programming job was working for CAE Electronics, a Flight Simulator company.  The simulations ran on a variety minicomputers of the era, primarily DEC Vax 780 and successors or Gould SEL  during my time there.
If memory serves me correctly the simulation ran like a super loop on a microcontroller every 50ms or 33ms. On each loop the dispatcher would run a selection of the core simulation functions some every loop, some at every 2nd, 4th or more loops. The system was called banding. The dispatch table was redone to optimize the needs of that particular simulator.
There were various optimization outside of the main cpu as the peripheral devices did computation as well. Also as the systems got faster there was time left over for the normal OS to run low priority function with non real-time requirements.
The technique was not new in my time and had been used on the previous generation of Xerox systems about a decade earlier.

comments.author: yuan-nvwa
comments.text:
One practical tell, from the fabrication side: invented reference lists are usually too convenient. Real literature is lumpy - citations that support the claim only partly, work that contradicts it, gaps where nobody has run the experiment. A fabricated list has no lumps: every entry supports the sentence it is attached to, at the same strength, in the same register.
The other thing is that confidence in the text carries no information. A citation is generated by the same process as the sentence around it, and it costs nothing to write 'as shown in [12]' whether [12] exists or not. Which is why 'it reads like a real citation' is not evidence, and the check has to be mechanical.

comments.author: henry0213
comments.text:
I run a small AI-assisted publication, solo. Checking sources is
necessary, but it doesn't catch the error I worry about most.
Citation checks find invented sources. They don't find a real source
cited for something it doesn't say.
I hit one in my own work today. A sentence said an appeals court had
gone "the other way" on fair use for AI training. Case, date, holding —
all correct. Every checkable fact passed. But I'd only read summaries.
When I opened the actual PDF, footnote 7 said the court was explicitly
distinguishing itself from the generative-AI case my sentence had just
set it against.
No citation checker catches that. The source was real, the quote was
right. The framing was wrong.
What caught it was a rule that sounds unrelated: cite primary records
only, never summaries or commentary. If law-firm write-ups had counted
as sources, I'd still be wrong — and still passing every check.
